qs.q: A 52-year-old woman presents for elective open cholecystectomy following multiple episodes of symptomatic cholelithiasis. Physical examination shows mild right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. Which of the following surgical incisions provides optimal exposure for this procedure?
qs.e: A right subcostal (Kocher) incision provides direct, optimal exposure to the gallbladder and biliary tree in the right upper quadrant. An upper midline incision can access the upper abdomen but offers inferior lateral visualization of the cystic duct and artery.

qs.q: An open cholecystectomy is planned for a patient with symptomatic cholelithiasis. Which specialized abdominal incision is most appropriate to provide direct access to the gallbladder and biliary tree?
qs.e: Kocher's right subcostal incision provides excellent access to the right upper quadrant structures such as the gallbladder and biliary tree during an open cholecystectomy. A Chevron incision is reserved for major upper abdominal procedures involving the liver and pancreas.
qs.s: Basic Surgical Skills: Scrubbing, Sutures, Knots, Incisions,: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain six months after undergoing a distal gastrectomy with Billroth II reconstruction. Ultrasound reveals gallbladder cholelithiasis without acute cholecystitis. Which physiological mechanism post-gastrectomy primarily promotes this condition?
qs.e: Truncal vagotomy and disrupted duodenal transit following gastrectomy impair postprandial CCK release, leading to gallbladder stasis and stone formation. Bilirubin hypersecretion is associated with hemolytic disorders rather than gastrectomy.

ai.title: Cholelithiasis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Gallstones form from cholesterol or pigment, most often in the gallbladder. They can be silent or cause biliary colic, cholecystitis or pancreatitis. Management balances surgery, drugs and local resources.

sections.p: Cholelithiasis is the presence of stones in the gallbladder or bile ducts. Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging, usually ultrasound, the test of choice in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Detects stones, gallbladder wall thickening, sludge; a single echogenic focus with acoustic shadowing is diagnostic.
Elevated ALP and GGT suggest biliary obstruction; normal bilirubin in early disease.
Leukocytosis indicates acute inflammation; anemia may hint at chronic hemolysis.

sections.p: Acute uncomplicated cholecystitis is stage I; gangrenous or perforated disease is stage III. Chronic cholelithiasis is asymptomatic or causes intermittent biliary colic.

t.b: Classify acute cholecystitis into mild, moderate, severe based on organ dysfunction and imaging.

sections.p: The classic risk factors are the 5 F’s: female, fat, fertile, forty, and former smoker. In East Africa, hemolytic disorders, malaria, and herbal hepatotoxins add risk.

t.b: Increased bilirubin leads to pigment stone formation.
Chronic hemolysis and hepatic congestion promote stone formation.
Some contain bile‑stimulatory compounds that precipitate cholesterol.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or have episodic right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, nausea, vomiting, or low‑grade fever. Acute cholecystitis presents with fever, tenderness, Murphy’s sign.
b: Right upper quadrant pain, often radiating to the shoulder

t.b: Pain on inspiration during right upper quadrant palpation indicates gallbladder inflammation.

sections.p: Ultrasound is first line. When unavailable, a plain abdominal X‑ray may show a calcified stone (rare). Lab tests guide severity.

t.b: Detects stones, gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid; confirms diagnosis.
Elevated ALP/GGT suggests obstruction; bilirubin rise indicates cholestasis.
Leukocytosis signals acute inflammation; anemia may suggest chronic hemolysis.

sections.p: Urgent complications include perforation, gangrene, sepsis, pancreatitis and choledocholithiasis. Watch for fever, tachycardia, hypotension, jaundice and worsening pain.

t.b: Suggests common bile duct stone; requires urgent drainage.

sections.p: Treat the cause first: antibiotics for infection, fluids for dehydration. Definitive treatment is cholecystectomy; in low‑resource settings, laparoscopic surgery is preferred if available. Non‑surgical options include oral dissolution therapy (ursodeoxycholic acid) for cholesterol stones, but requires long course and monitoring.
b: Antibiotics – broad spectrum covering gram‑negative and anaerobes

t.b: Used for small cholesterol stones; reduces stone size over months.
Temporary drainage for high‑risk surgical patients.

sections.p: After surgery, advise weight control, balanced diet, and avoidance of rapid weight loss. In chronic hemolytic states, monitor for gallstones with periodic ultrasound.

t.b: Repeat every 6–12 months in high‑risk patients.

faq.q: Why is a low‑fat diet not recommended for gallstone prevention?
faq.a: A low‑fat diet reduces gallbladder contraction, increasing stasis and stone risk.
No; they treat infection but do not dissolve stones.

faq.q: What is the safest drug for dissolving cholesterol stones?
faq.a: Ursodeoxycholic acid, given orally, is the only approved medical therapy.

exam: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal. What is the first investigation? — Ultrasound to confirm stones and assess gallbladder wall thickness.
A patient with cholelithiasis has a sudden rise in bilirubin and jaundice. What is the next step? — Immediate ERCP or surgical drainage of the common bile duct.
Why is a high‑dose proton pump inhibitor not useful in gallstone disease? — It does not affect stone formation or biliary inflammation.
A patient with chronic hemolytic anemia develops gallstones. Which complication is most likely? — Acute cholecystitis due to gallbladder stasis.
In a low‑resource setting, a patient has acute cholecystitis but no operating theatre. What is the best interim management? — Percutaneous cholecystostomy to drain the gallbladder.
What laboratory value would most strongly suggest acute cholangitis? — Bilirubin >3 mg/dL with elevated ALP and GGT.
